g9-civics-uc3-t1.overview: A constitution is the supreme law of a state: a fundamental document that defines the nature of government and the rights and duties of citizens. This lesson defines the constitution, classifies its types, and explains the basic principles on which it rests.
objectives: Define constitution as the supreme law of a state
List the main types of constitution
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of written and unwritten constitutions
Describe the fundamental principles of a constitution
Explain how a constitution limits government and protects citizens
g9-civics-uc3-t1.simple: A constitution is the fundamental document that contains the basic laws of a country. It is the supreme law of the state, and it defines the nature of government, its functions, and the rights and duties of citizens. Constitutions are classified in three ways: written or unwritten, rigid or flexible, and federal or unitary. A written constitution is codified in a single document and is easy for citizens to read, but it is rigid. An unwritten constitution lives in customs and conventions and is easy to change, but it is hard for citizens to access. A federal constitution shares power between federal and regional governments, while a unitary one keeps power at the centre. Every constitution also carries principles such as popular sovereignty, limited government and rule of law.
g9-civics-uc3-t1.detailed:
What a constitution is. A constitution is a fundamental document that contains the basic laws of a country. It is the most fundamental or supreme law of a state and underlines the very existence of the state. It is the aggregate of laws, customs, conventions, principles, rules and regulations by which a particular government of a country implements its administrative activities. A constitution defines the nature of the government and its functions, and it declares the rights and duties of citizens.

Written and unwritten constitutions. A written constitution exists in a single document or in a codified form, and it clearly lays down the fundamental rules about the nature of government and the rights and duties of citizens. It is precise, definite and systematic, and the majority of states have one, for example Ethiopia, South Africa, Nigeria, India, the United States of America, France and Brazil. An unwritten constitution is not found in a single written document; instead it exists in the form of customs and conventions. It is unsystematic, indefinite and imprecise, and only a few countries have one, for instance the United Kingdom and Israel.

Advantages and disadvantages. A written constitution is easily accessible to citizens, who can get it from a library, from other individuals, from online, or buy it from a bookshop, and it enables them to learn their rights and duties easily. Its main limitation is rigidity: compared with an unwritten constitution, it is not easy to improve in changing circumstances. An unwritten constitution is simple and easy to amend because it is undocumented or uncodified, but it is not easily accessible and citizens do not have the chance to learn about their rights and duties from a constitutional document.

Rigid and flexible constitutions. Amendment procedure refers to modifying the constitution, adding important issues to it or removing unimportant ones. A rigid constitution cannot be amended in the manner in which ordinary laws are passed, amended or repealed; it requires special or difficult procedures for the amendment process, for example the constitutions of Ethiopia and the United States of America. A flexible constitution is simple for amendment and can be changed by an ordinary legislative process or by ordinary resolution; it does not require a special procedure, for example the constitutions of Britain and Israel.

Federal and unitary constitutions. A federal constitution distributes power between the federal and the regional governments, for example the 1995 FDRE constitution. A unitary constitution centralizes all state power at the central government, for example the constitution of Britain.

Fundamental principles. A constitution rests on certain fundamental principles. Popular sovereignty refers to the ultimate or supreme power of the people: the people are the ultimate source of power and the government must be based on their consent. Limited government means the power of government must be limited by the constitution, so that it acts according to the power and functions given to it. Separation of powers assigns specific responsibilities and powers to each branch of government, such as the legislative, executive and judiciary organs, for a system of check and balance. Rule of law means everyone acts according to the law; the law applies to everyone, even to those who are in power. Respect for human rights means the human rights of individuals or groups must be respected by both the government and ordinary citizens. Transparency and accountability means the conduct and actions of government officials must be open to the public, and officials must be held responsible for any failure in their official duties.

Why it matters. The constitution is the highest and fundamental law of a state. It is very important to ensure the rule of law and to put the government within its limit. Because it is the supreme standard, every other law and every official act must comply with it.

keyTerms.def: The fundamental document that contains the basic laws of a country; the supreme law of a state, defining the nature of government and the rights and duties of citizens.
A constitution that exists in a single document or in a codified form, laying down the fundamental rules clearly and precisely.
A constitution that is not found in a single written document but exists in the form of customs and conventions.
A constitution that requires special or difficult procedures for the amendment process, such as those of Ethiopia and the United States.
A constitution that is simple for amendment and can be changed by an ordinary legislative process, such as those of Britain and Israel.
A constitution that distributes power between the federal and the regional governments, for example the 1995 FDRE constitution.
A constitution that centralizes all state power at the central government, for example the constitution of Britain.
The ultimate or supreme power of the people; the people are the ultimate source of power and government rests on their consent.

workedExamples.problem: Parliament passes an ordinary law that allows the executive to keep information about citizens secret. A citizen argues that the constitution is the supreme law. Which law should prevail and why?
workedExamples.given: The ordinary law was passed by parliament, but it conflicts with a fundamental right in the constitution.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the constitution is the highest and fundamental law of the state and limits the power of government.
workedExamples.substitution: An ordinary law that contradicts the constitution is acting outside the power the constitution gives it.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the constitution is supreme, every other law must comply with it, so the conflicting ordinary law cannot stand.
workedExamples.answer: The constitution prevails; the ordinary law is invalid because it violates the supreme law.

workedExamples.problem: A student in Addis Ababa wants to read the exact rights promised to citizens. Should she look for a written or an unwritten constitution, and why?
workedExamples.given: She needs a single, definite source that she can read and quote.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a written constitution is codified, precise, definite and systematic.
workedExamples.substitution: A written constitution collects the fundamental rules in one document that citizens can access in a library or online.
workedExamples.calculation: An unwritten constitution exists only in customs and conventions and is not easily accessible, so it cannot give her a definite text.
workedExamples.answer: A written constitution; it is precise and easy for citizens to access.

workedExamples.problem: Country A amends its constitution by an ordinary act of parliament, while Country B requires a special procedure. Classify both constitutions.
workedExamples.given: Country A uses the ordinary legislative process; Country B requires special or difficult procedures.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: based on amendment procedure a constitution is rigid when it needs special procedure or flexible when an ordinary process is enough.
workedExamples.substitution: Country A matches the definition of flexible; Country B matches the definition of rigid.
workedExamples.calculation: Ethiopia and the United States have rigid constitutions, while Britain and Israel have flexible ones.
workedExamples.answer: Country A has a flexible constitution; Country B has a rigid constitution.

workedExamples.problem: A regional government decides to print its own currency and conduct its own foreign policy, saying the constitution allows it. Using the principle of limited government, evaluate this.
workedExamples.given: The region is acting outside the powers the constitution gives to regional governments.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: limited government means acting only according to the power and functions given by the constitution.
workedExamples.substitution: A federal constitution distributes power between federal and regional governments, and currency and foreign policy belong to the federal government.
workedExamples.calculation: The region is exceeding its constitutional powers, so the action fails the test of limited government.
workedExamples.answer: The action is unconstitutional; regional power must stay within the constitution.

commonMistakes: Thinking a constitution is just another ordinary law of the land.
Believing an unwritten constitution does not really exist because it is not written down.
Assuming a written constitution has no disadvantages at all.
Confusing a federal constitution with a unitary one; only a federal constitution shares power with the regions.
Thinking a rigid constitution can be amended by the same ordinary process as an ordinary law.
Believing the constitution limits only citizens and not the government.
applications: Reading chapter three of the 1995 FDRE constitution to learn the rights of citizens.
Asking your local government office for a copy of the constitution instead of relying on rumour.
Explaining to your family why a government decision that breaks the constitution cannot stand.
Discussing in class how the federal constitution shares power between the federal and the regional governments.
Refusing to obey an unlawful instruction from an official, because the constitution is supreme.
g9-civics-uc3-t1.summary: A constitution is the fundamental and supreme law of a state. It defines the nature of government and the rights and duties of citizens. Constitutions are classified as written or unwritten, rigid or flexible, and federal or unitary. Every constitution rests on fundamental principles such as popular sovereignty, limited government, separation of powers, rule of law, respect for human rights, and transparency and accountability.

g9-civics-uc3-t2.overview: Constitutionalism is a government system that is based on and acts according to the supreme law, not merely the existence of a constitution. This lesson explains what constitutionalism means, why it matters, and what a limited government by law looks like.
objectives: Distinguish having a constitution from practising constitutionalism
Identify the features of a limited government by law
Explain how constitutionalism prevents tyranny and the abuse of power
g9-civics-uc3-t2.simple: Constitutionalism means a government system that is based on and acts according to the supreme law. It is not enough for a country to have a constitution on paper; the government and its agents must actually follow the fundamental principles of that constitution. Constitutionalism implies a limited system of government by law in which the real rights and freedoms of citizens are realized, good governance is practised, the rule of law prevails, and powers are separated. It prevents tyranny and guarantees liberty. It controls the abuse and misuse of government power, because officials must conduct public duties according to the law. It also makes the rule of law prevail, so that everyone, including those in power, obeys the law and no one is above it.
g9-civics-uc3-t2.detailed:
What constitutionalism means. Constitutionalism refers to a government system that is based on and acts according to the supreme law. It implies a limited system of government by law in which there is an actual or real realization of the fundamental rights and freedoms of citizens, a real practice of good governance, rule of law and separation of powers.

Constitution is not enough. Having a constitution on paper does not by itself mean that constitutionalism exists. According to the notion of constitutionalism, the behaviour and actions of the government as well as its agents should be founded on the fundamental principles of the constitution. Constitutionalism is therefore beyond merely having a constitution: it is all about the real implementation of those fundamental principles, and it is against any arbitrary or undemocratic system of government.

Realization of human rights. Human rights are inviolable and inalienable rights. Constitutionalism prevents tyranny and guarantees the liberty and rights of individuals or groups of individuals. Respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms for all is the responsibility of every citizen and of the government in particular, and this can become real only when there is a government which acts according to the supreme law.

Controlling the abuse and misuse of power. Constitutionalism checks whether the acts of a government are legitimate, and whether officials conduct their public duties in accordance with the law. It provides institutional safeguards against the abuse and misuse of powers by authorities, so that power is not turned against the people it is meant to serve.

Prevalence of the rule of law. Constitutionalism is a foundation for the rule of law. It proclaims the necessity of the rule of law in contrast to rule by arbitrary judgment. Everyone must be a law abiding citizen: citizens must accept the limits on their freedom, and officials must also observe the limits on their power.

Limited government by law. A limited government is one that acts only according to the power and functions given to it by the constitution. It is the opposite of an unlimited or arbitrary government, in which rulers decide for themselves how far their power reaches. A real practice of constitutionalism has a remarkable contribution and is usually at the forefront in insuring peace and stability and human well-being.

keyTerms.def: A government system that is based on and acts according to the supreme law, with a real practice of good governance, rule of law and separation of powers.
A government that acts according to the power and functions given to it by the constitution.
The principle that everyone acts according to the law and no one, not even those in power, is above it.
Cruel and arbitrary rule by a leader or group that is not limited by law; constitutionalism prevents it.
Inviolable and inalienable rights of individuals or groups that constitutionalism guarantees and protects.
The distribution of power among the legislative, executive and judiciary branches for the purpose of check and balance.
The use of public authority for purposes other than those allowed by law; constitutionalism provides safeguards against it.
The condition in which government officials are held responsible for any failure in their official duties.

workedExamples.problem: Country X has a beautifully written constitution, but its leaders ignore it, arrest critics and rule by their own orders. Does constitutionalism exist there?
workedExamples.given: A constitution exists on paper, but the government does not act according to it.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: constitutionalism requires the actual realization of the fundamental principles of the constitution.
workedExamples.substitution: Ruling by personal orders is rule by arbitrary judgment, not by the supreme law.
workedExamples.calculation: The behaviour of the government is not founded on the constitution, so the paper document alone does not produce constitutionalism.
workedExamples.answer: No. The country has a constitution but no constitutionalism.

workedExamples.problem: A minister awards a large contract to a relative and refuses to explain the decision. Which aspects of constitutionalism are violated?
workedExamples.given: Public duties are not conducted according to the law, and the decision is not open to the public.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: constitutionalism controls the abuse of power and requires transparency and accountability.
workedExamples.substitution: Nepotism is an abuse of power, and secrecy violates transparency and accountability.
workedExamples.calculation: Both the safeguard against abuse of power and the requirement of openness fail.
workedExamples.answer: Abuse of power, lack of transparency and lack of accountability are all violated.

workedExamples.problem: A police officer says that senior officials are above the law. Using constitutionalism, respond.
workedExamples.given: The officer claims that people in power need not obey the law.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: constitutionalism proclaims the rule of law, in which everyone must be law abiding and no one is above the law.
workedExamples.substitution: The claim contradicts the rule of law, which applies equally to citizens and to officials.
workedExamples.calculation: Officials must observe the limits on their power, so no office holder is above the law.
workedExamples.answer: The officer is wrong; the rule of law applies to everyone, even those in power.

workedExamples.problem: Compare a limited government with an unlimited government in a scenario where a leader wants to rule without elections.
workedExamples.given: In one system the leader needs the consent of the people; in the other the leader rules alone.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a limited government acts according to the power given by the constitution and rests on the consent of the people.
workedExamples.substitution: Ruling without elections is rule by arbitrary judgment and ignores popular sovereignty.
workedExamples.calculation: The system that requires consent and obeys the constitution is limited; the other is unlimited.
workedExamples.answer: The limited government obeys the constitution and the people; the unlimited one does not.

commonMistakes: Believing that having a constitution automatically means that constitutionalism exists.
Thinking a limited government is a weak government.
Assuming officials are above the law once they hold power.
Confusing the rule of law with rule by the personal judgment of leaders.
Believing constitutionalism only protects citizens and not the limits on officials.
Thinking human rights are privileges that the government may grant or withdraw at will.
applications: Demanding that a public office explain a decision that affects your kebele, because of accountability.
Refusing to join a group that wants to settle a dispute by force instead of by the rule of law.
Reporting an official who abuses power to the relevant body instead of staying silent.
Discussing in a civics club how constitutionalism prevents tyranny and protects freedom.
Respecting the limits on your own freedom, for example by not harming the rights of others.
g9-civics-uc3-t2.summary: Constitutionalism is a government system based on and acting according to the supreme law, not merely the existence of a constitution. It implies limited government by law, the real realization of human rights, good governance, rule of law and separation of powers. It prevents tyranny, controls the abuse and misuse of power, and makes the rule of law prevail so that no one, including officials, is above the law.

g9-civics-uc3-t3.overview: Ethiopia has a long history of constitutional experience, from traditional documents before 1931 to the 1995 FDRE constitution. This lesson traces that journey and identifies the fundamental principles of the present constitution.
objectives: Describe Ethiopia's traditional constitutional experiences before 1931
Outline the main features of the 1931 and 1955 imperial constitutions
Explain the 1987 PDRE constitution and the constitutional vacuum of 1974 to 1987
Describe the 1991 Transitional Charter and the 1995 FDRE constitution
Identify the fundamental constitutional principles of the 1995 FDRE constitution
g9-civics-uc3-t3.simple: Ethiopia has a long history of constitutional experience. Until the early 1930s the emperors ruled under traditional documents such as Kibre Negest, Fetha Negest and Sirate Mengist, which gave the monarch legitimacy rather than protecting the rights of citizens. The first written constitution was granted by Emperor Haile Selassie I in 1931, followed by a revised constitution in 1955; both aimed to strengthen the power of the emperor. After the Derg took power in 1974 there was a constitutional vacuum until the 1987 PDRE constitution, which created a republican government and introduced secularism. The 1991 Transitional Charter served until the 1995 FDRE constitution, which introduced a federal structure and a parliamentary democracy with two houses of parliament.
g9-civics-uc3-t3.detailed:
A long constitutional history. Ethiopia is a country that has a long history of constitutional experiences. It used traditional or unwritten constitutions until the introduction of the first written constitution by Emperor Haile Selassie I in 1931.

Traditional constitutional experiences. Until the early 1930s, the rule of the Ethiopian emperors was based on traditional constitutions such as Kibre Negest, Fetha Negest and Sirate Mengist. This experience was characterized by the dominance of myths and legends that were used to provide legitimacy to the monarchs rather than ensuring the basic rights and freedoms of citizens. The Kibre Negest (Glory of Kings) justifies that the Ethiopian monarchs derived their power to rule from God. The Fetha Negest (Law of Kings) justifies the authority of kings and their officials; according to it, challenging the authority of the king is considered as challenging or rebelling against one's creator, God. Sirate Mengist, which emerged in the nineteenth century, proved to be an administrative and protocol directive of the government.

The 1931 and 1955 imperial constitutions. The first written constitution was granted to the people on July 16, 1931, a few months after the coronation of Emperor Haile Selassie I. The Emperor was motivated mainly by two reasons: his high aspiration to show Ethiopia as a modern or civilized state to the external world, and the wish to consolidate his absolute power over local nobilities through a formal constitutional framework. The constitution had 7 chapters and 55 articles, and its principal aim was to consolidate the power of the king, not to lay foundations for the fundamental rights and dignity of citizens. The revised constitution of 1955 was adopted mainly for internal and external reasons. The internal reason was the Italian invasion of Ethiopia in 1935, which interrupted the 1931 constitution and forced the Emperor to flee to Britain; the external and most basic reason was the federation of Eritrea with Ethiopia in 1952. The 1955 revised constitution had 8 chapters and 131 articles, but it still did not limit the power of the Emperor and prominent officials, and the democratic and human rights of citizens were not guaranteed.

The 1987 PDRE constitution. In 1974 the feudal monarchy, or imperial regime, was removed from power by the Derg military regime. The Derg introduced decrees and proclamations that had no constitutional status until the adoption of the 1987 constitution, so the period from 1974 up to 1987 is known as a constitutional vacuum or lacuna in Ethiopian political history. The 1987 constitution had 7 chapters and 119 articles. It changed the system of government from the monarchy system to a republican form of government, and it introduced the idea of secularism, or the separation of state and religion, for the first time in Ethiopia. Like its predecessors, it left no legacy of a democratic constitutional order. After staying in power for 17 years, the Derg regime led by Colonel Mengistu Hailemariam was overthrown by the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front in May 1991.

The 1991 Transitional Charter. The 1991 Transitional Charter was introduced in May 1991 by the EPRDF after the demise of the Derg regime, and it served as the law of the land from 1991 up to 1995. It is a very short document of only 20 articles that addressed only some fundamental issues. The charter recognized the freedom, equal right and self-determination of all nationalities, and it put a high premium on human rights.

The 1995 FDRE constitution. The period of the Transitional Charter ended with the adoption of the FDRE constitution in December 1995. It introduced different changes compared with its predecessors: a federal state structure for the first time, parliamentary democracy, and the establishment of the two houses of parliament, the House of Federation and the House of People's Representatives. It also guarantees the rights and freedoms of citizens and describes the duties of citizens. The 1995 constitution has a preamble and 11 chapters with 106 articles.

Fundamental principles of the 1995 FDRE constitution. These are popular sovereignty (Article 8), supremacy of the constitution (Article 9), respecting human and democratic rights (Article 10), secularism or separation of state and religion (Article 11), and transparency and accountability of government (Article 12). Although Ethiopia has long constitutional experience, it does not have a good history and culture of constitutionalism.

keyTerms.def: A traditional document (Glory of Kings) that justified that the Ethiopian monarchs derived their power to rule from God.
A traditional document (Law of Kings) that justified the authority of kings and their officials.
A nineteenth century document that served as an administrative and protocol directive of the government.
The period from 1974 to 1987 when the Derg ruled by decrees and proclamations that had no constitutional status; also called a lacuna.
The 1991 charter of 20 articles that served as the law of the land from 1991 up to 1995.
The separation of state and religion, introduced for the first time in Ethiopia by the 1987 PDRE constitution.
The 1995 constitution with a preamble and 11 chapters and 106 articles that introduced the federal state structure.
One of the two houses of parliament established by the 1995 FDRE constitution, alongside the House of People's Representatives.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the main aim of the 1931 constitution with that of the 1995 FDRE constitution.
workedExamples.given: The 1931 constitution had 7 chapters and 55 articles; the 1995 FDRE constitution has a preamble and 11 chapters with 106 articles.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a constitution may either entrench the power of a ruler or lay foundations for the rights of citizens and limited government.
workedExamples.substitution: The 1931 constitution consolidated the absolute power of the emperor, while the 1995 constitution guarantees rights and establishes federalism.
workedExamples.calculation: The 1931 aim fails the test of constitutionalism because it did not protect rights, while the 1995 aim moves toward it.
workedExamples.answer: 1931 strengthened the power of the emperor; 1995 protects rights and limits government through federalism.

workedExamples.problem: Between 1974 and 1987 the Derg ruled by decrees and proclamations. What was the constitutional situation in Ethiopia then?
workedExamples.given: The Derg issued decrees and proclamations that had no constitutional status until 1987.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a constitutional vacuum or lacuna is a period without a constitution of the land.
workedExamples.substitution: The interval between the end of the imperial constitution and the 1987 PDRE constitution had no constitutional status.
workedExamples.calculation: That interval matches the definition of a constitutional vacuum.
workedExamples.answer: It was a constitutional vacuum, or lacuna, from 1974 to 1987.

workedExamples.problem: A researcher asks which Ethiopian constitution first introduced secularism and which first introduced federalism. Answer both.
workedExamples.given: The 1987 PDRE constitution and the 1995 FDRE constitution are the candidates.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: match each document with the change that it introduced.
workedExamples.substitution: Secularism, the separation of state and religion, was introduced by the 1987 PDRE constitution, while the federal state structure was introduced by the 1995 FDRE constitution.
workedExamples.calculation: Each change belongs to the constitution named in the lesson, so the match is clear.
workedExamples.answer: Secularism: the 1987 PDRE constitution. Federalism: the 1995 FDRE constitution.

workedExamples.problem: The traditional constitutions claimed that rulers received power from God. Evaluate whether this practise meets the idea of constitutionalism.
workedExamples.given: Kibre Negest and Fetha Negest were used to give legitimacy to the monarch rather than to protect rights.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: constitutionalism limits government power by law and protects the rights and freedoms of citizens.
workedExamples.substitution: Unlimited, divinely justified rule is the opposite of limited government and popular sovereignty.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the documents did not limit the ruler or protect basic rights, they fail the test of constitutionalism.
workedExamples.answer: No. They justified absolute rule and did not practise constitutionalism.

commonMistakes: Thinking Ethiopia has a long history of constitutionalism because it has a long history of constitutions.
Believing the 1931 constitution was meant to protect the rights of citizens.
Assuming the imperial constitutions limited the power of the emperor.
Confusing the 1987 PDRE constitution with the 1995 FDRE constitution.
Calling the period from 1974 to 1987 a constitution when it was a constitutional vacuum.
Thinking secularism was first introduced by the 1995 FDRE constitution rather than by the 1987 PDRE constitution.
applications: Reading the 1995 FDRE constitution and listing its five fundamental principles with their article numbers.
Preparing a class timeline of Ethiopian constitutions from 1931 to 1995.
Debating in class why the 1931 and 1955 constitutions failed to protect the rights of citizens.
Explaining how the federal structure created in 1995 affects the government of your own region.
Discussing why a country needs not only constitutions but also a culture of constitutionalism.
g9-civics-uc3-t3.summary: Ethiopia has a long constitutional history, from traditional documents such as Kibre Negest, Fetha Negest and Sirate Mengist to the first written constitution of 1931. The 1931 and 1955 imperial constitutions mainly strengthened the power of the emperor, the Derg period brought a constitutional vacuum and then the 1987 PDRE constitution, and the 1991 Transitional Charter led to the 1995 FDRE constitution. The 1995 constitution introduced federalism and parliamentary democracy and rests on fundamental principles such as popular sovereignty, supremacy of the constitution and respect for human rights.

questions.q: The 1995 FDRE constitution introduced for the first time:
questions.explanation: The 1995 FDRE constitution introduced a federal state structure for the first time.

questions.q: Ethiopia has a long history of constitutionalism along with its long constitutional experience.
questions.explanation: Although Ethiopia has long constitutional experience, it does not have a good history and culture of constitutionalism.

questions.q: Arrange these Ethiopian constitutional milestones in the correct chronological order, starting with the earliest.
questions.explanation: The order is 1931, 1987, 1991 Transitional Charter, then 1995 FDRE constitution, so the earliest is the 1931 written constitution.

questions.q: Give two fundamental constitutional principles of the 1995 FDRE constitution.
questions.answer: popular sovereignty|supremacy of the constitution|respecting human and democratic rights|secularism|transparency and accountability
questions.explanation: The principles are popular sovereignty, supremacy of the constitution, respect for human and democratic rights, secularism, and transparency and accountability.

questions.q: The 1955 revised constitution had:
questions.explanation: The 1955 revised constitution had 8 chapters and 131 articles.
